text:
Recent work supports combining item text with collaborative sequences, but does not establish a clear lightweight, from-scratch solution matching all constraints. [AlterRec (2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.ijcnlp-long.12.pdf) finds that joint ID–text fusion can undertrain text because IDs dominate optimization; alternating their optimization improves integration. [DeCoRec (2025)](https://cwang-zju.github.io/files/mm25.pdf) similarly identifies unequal convergence rates and proposes training modality representations first, then freezing them while refining collaborative embeddings. These findings motivate separate optimization schedules; they do not establish that pretrained-free title/description encoders will improve this benchmark.

[Sequence-level Semantic Representation Fusion (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18166) argues that directly adding text and ID embeddings can be ineffective, proposing contextual fusion through Fourier-domain operations. A [2026 adaptive-fusion model](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-026-00562-4) combines collaborative and semantic embeddings, but explicitly requires pretrained language-model features, making its implementation incompatible with the stated restrictions.

Practical hypothesis, rather than a verified literature result: retain SASRec and add a small randomly initialized token-embedding encoder over permitted titles/descriptions, using pooled tokens or a shallow CNN. Train with next-item supervision and optionally a modest text–ID alignment loss; compare joint training against text warm-up or alternating updates. Gate the text contribution using observed text availability and training interaction counts, with zero contribution for missing text. Validate against ID-only and ungated fusion using the common macro HR@10. Lexical similarity may support shared attributes or purposes explicitly mentioned in text; it does not establish product compatibility, functional substitutability, or unobserved user traits.
